title: Secondary findings in adult clinical genomic sequencing
short_description: An adult undergoes clinical genomic sequencing for a diagnostic indication. The health system must choose how intentionally sought, medically actionable secondary findings are analyzed and offered.
decision_question: What policy should a health system use for medically actionable secondary findings unrelated to the original reason for adult exome/genome sequencing?
jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral adult clinical genomics policy, evidence-dated 2026.

stipulations.statement: Any secondary finding returned to the patient would be analytically confirmed and clinically interpreted.
stipulations.rationale: The case concerns consent architecture for actionable findings rather than false-positive laboratory reporting.

stipulations.statement: Pre- and post-test genetic counseling is available.
stipulations.rationale: Counseling capacity is held fixed so opt-in/opt-out differences are not proxies for unequal informed-consent support.

stipulations.statement: The represented secondary findings concern serious conditions with established surveillance, preventive treatment or other interventions that can meaningfully reduce morbidity or mortality.
stipulations.rationale: The natural policy disagreement concerns actionable secondary findings; nonactionable risk information would create a different case.

position_families: default analysis and return of a defined actionable set with informed opt-out
restrict diagnostic analysis to the clinical indication rather than routinely seek unrelated findings
routine analysis limited to a higher penetrance/actionability threshold

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored adult clinical-genomics representation synthesized from divergent professional secondary-findings policies and patient-preference evidence. It fixes analytic confirmation, counseling and clinically actionable conditions so the represented variable is whether unrelated actionable findings are deliberately sought and, if so, under what consent architecture.

public.text: Analyze a defined set of medically actionable secondary findings by default and offer return with genetic counseling unless the patient makes an informed choice to opt out before analysis.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference: patient studies show very high demand for medically actionable secondary findings. Those preferences support a return-oriented policy but do not directly establish an opt-out default.

public.text: Do not analyze unrelated secondary findings until the patient affirmatively authorizes the categories they wish to receive; apply that choice before secondary analysis begins.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference: public and patient studies repeatedly emphasize choice about whether and which secondary findings to receive. The Bench translates that preference structure into a pre-analysis opt-in architecture rather than claiming respondents directly endorsed this institutional rule.

expert.text: Offer analysis and return of a professionally defined minimum list of medically actionable secondary findings with informed opt-out, confirmatory interpretation and appropriate genetic counseling.

provenance.summary: Adapted from ACMG's current secondary-findings architecture: a defined minimum list of actionable gene–disease pairs is intentionally analyzed in clinical sequencing while patients retain an informed opportunity to opt out; list content is updated as evidence changes. Two further ACMG positions are declared because they bear on other candidates here and this one does not carry them. ACMG explicitly rejects an opt-in default — "providing the opportunity for an informed decision and opt out, if desired, at the time of consent should continue to be the standard" — which is a stated position against pub2 and fw2 rather than mere absence of support. And ACMG recommends "avoiding inclusion of gene–phenotype pairs with uncertain or lower penetrance estimates," preferring pairs with "a higher likelihood that the individual will manifest the phenotype" — a version of the high-penetrance threshold fw3 derives from principle. fw3 therefore has professional support as well as a framework derivation, and a reader should not take it as unsupported by the expert layer.

expert.text: Do not routinely use a diagnostic exome or genome as an opportunity to search for unrelated secondary findings; where possible, restrict analysis to regions relevant to the clinical indication and consider additional screening only under separately justified, proportionate and consented programs.

provenance.summary: Adapted from ESHG recommendations that diagnostic genome analysis should, where possible, be restricted to the health problem that prompted testing and that opportunistic genomic screening requires separate justification in terms of proportionality, autonomy and resources. International policy review confirms that some professional bodies actively discourage intentional analysis of secondary findings even when actionable.

framework.text: Analyze highly actionable findings by default with an opt-out because preventable serious disease supplies a strong reason to make beneficial risk information available unless the patient refuses it.

provenance.summary: Derived from beneficence and prevention: when clinically valid information can enable meaningful prevention or surveillance, a default offer can protect health while an opt-out preserves refusal. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

sources.citation: Miller DT, et al. ACMG secondary-findings policy, 2021 update.

framework.text: Generate unrelated genomic risk information only after explicit patient authorization because deciding whether that information should exist is itself part of informational self-determination.

provenance.summary: Derived from informational autonomy and the right-not-to-know tradition: autonomy can concern whether unwanted genetic information is generated and disclosed, not merely whether it is received after analysis. The executable rule is a Bench construction.

sources.citation: Andorno R. The right not to know: an autonomy based approach. J Med Ethics. 2004;30(5):435–439. PMID 15467071.

framework.text: Routine secondary analysis should be limited to findings meeting a particularly high threshold of penetrance and clinical actionability, reducing avoidable diagnostic cascades and burdens even when a broader list could technically be analyzed.

provenance.summary: Derived from proportionality and epistemic restraint: the case for deliberately seeking unrelated information strengthens with clinical validity, predictive value and available intervention, while lower-yield findings create greater risk of cascades and burden. The policy sentence is a Bench construction.

representation.notes: Concise and detailed are companion representations of the same natural frame; candidate pools and load-bearing facts are fixed.

scenario: An adult with decision-making capacity is undergoing clinical exome/genome sequencing for a diagnostic indication. In addition to variants related to that indication, the laboratory can intentionally search for a predefined set of pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants associated with serious conditions for which surveillance, preventive treatment or another established intervention can meaningfully reduce morbidity or mortality. For this benchmark, assume every returned secondary finding would be analytically confirmed and clinically interpreted, pre- and post-test genetic counseling is available, and the represented conditions have established interventions; penetrance and actionability nevertheless vary across gene–disease pairs. The health system must choose a standing policy: routine secondary analysis with informed opt-out, secondary analysis only after explicit opt-in, restriction of diagnostic analysis to the clinical indication rather than routine opportunistic search, or a narrower secondary program restricted to findings meeting a particularly high threshold of penetrance and clinical actionability.
